lessons.title: Identifying Types of Stone and Mortar in Old Buildings
lessons.body:
Before you touch any old wall, you need to know what you're dealing with. In Africa, historic buildings often use local stone: sandstone in the Karoo, granite in Zimbabwe, coral rag along the Swahili coast, or laterite in West Africa. Each stone behaves differently. Sandstone is soft and porous; granite is hard and dense; coral is brittle and salty. Test with a pocket knife: if it scratches easily, it's soft. If it resists, it's hard. Also note colour and grain â sandstone has visible sand grains, granite has speckles of quartz and feldspar.

Mortar is just as important. Old mortars are usually lime-based: white or off-white, soft, and crumbly. They may contain sand, crushed brick, or ash. Cement mortar, by contrast, is grey, hard, and often cracked. Scratch the mortar with a nail: lime mortar powders easily; cement mortar resists. If you see Portland cement, it was likely added in the 20th century â often causing damage because it's harder than the stone.

To confirm, put a drop of vinegar on the mortar. If it fizzes, it's lime (calcium carbonate). If not, it's cement or gypsum. For stone, look for bedding planes â sedimentary stone like sandstone splits along layers. Igneous stone like granite is uniform. Metamorphic like slate is foliated.

Record your findings: take photos, label stone type, mortar type, and any previous repairs. This guide will dictate your cleaning, repointing, and replacement methods. Without this step, you risk using the wrong material and causing irreversible harm. In Africa, where traditional knowledge is fading, this identification is the first act of preservation.

lessons.title: Cleaning and Repointing Stone Walls
lessons.body:
Cleaning old stone walls requires patience. Never use a high-pressure washer â it blasts away the stone surface and drives water into cracks. Instead, start with a soft bristle brush and clean water. For stubborn dirt, use a wooden scraper. If you need a chemical, use a pH-neutral stone cleaner (like D/2) diluted 1:10. Apply with a brush, leave for 5 minutes, then scrub and rinse. For biological growth (algae, lichen), use a 1:1 mix of household bleach and water, but test on a hidden area first â bleach can bleach some stones.

Repointing is the art of replacing mortar joints. First, remove old mortar to a depth of 2-3 cm (about 1 inch) using a plugging chisel and mallet. Never use an angle grinder â it cuts into the stone edges. Work on one square metre at a time. Rake out the joint with a mortar rake or old screwdriver. Brush out dust with a stiff brush.

Mix lime mortar: 1 part hydraulic lime (NHL 3.5 or 5) to 2.5 parts sharp sand (0-4 mm). Add water gradually until it holds together like damp sand â not dripping. Let it sit for 10 minutes, then remix. Use a pointing trowel to press mortar into joints, filling them fully. Finish with a wooden stick or jointing tool to match the original profile â usually a concave or flush finish. Do not smooth with a metal trowel; it seals the surface and prevents breathability.

After pointing, keep the wall damp for 3 days by misting with water and covering with burlap. This slows curing and prevents cracking. In hot African climates, do this early morning and late afternoon. Repointing extends the life of a stone wall by decades.

lessons.title: Repairing Cracked or Missing Stones
lessons.body:
When a stone is cracked or missing, you must replace it. First, assess the damage: a hairline crack (less than 1 mm) can be left if it's stable. But a crack wider than 2 mm, or a missing stone, needs repair. Use a chisel and mallet to carefully remove the damaged stone. Work from the centre outwards to avoid damaging neighbours. For a missing stone, clean the cavity â remove all old mortar and dust. Measure the cavity: length, width, depth.

Source a replacement stone of the same type and hardness. In Africa, you can often find matching stone from local quarries or salvage yards. If not, use a compatible new stone â for sandstone, use a similar sandstone; for granite, use granite. Cut the new stone to size with a mason's chisel and angle grinder (with diamond blade). Leave a 5-10 mm gap around the edges for mortar. Soak the new stone in water for 30 minutes before setting â this prevents it from sucking moisture from the mortar.

Mix a lime mortar (1:2.5 NHL to sand) and apply a 10 mm bed. Press the stone into place with a rubber mallet. Check it's level and flush with the wall face. Fill joints with mortar, packing tightly. For cracked stones that you can't replace, inject a grout made of lime putty and fine sand (1:1) using a syringe. This fills the crack and consolidates the stone.

After repair, keep the area damp for 3 days. Avoid heavy loads for a week. In hot, dry regions, shade the repair from direct sun. Proper stone replacement maintains the structural integrity and appearance of historic walls.

lessons.title: Using Lime Mortar for Historic Masonry
lessons.body:
Lime mortar is the backbone of historic masonry restoration. Unlike cement, lime mortar is soft, breathable, and flexible. It allows moisture to evaporate from the wall, preventing salt damage and frost spalling. In Africa, where many old buildings are made of stone and lime, using cement is a common mistake that traps moisture and cracks the stone.

There are two main types: non-hydraulic lime (lime putty) and hydraulic lime (NHL). Non-hydraulic lime sets by carbonation â it reacts with CO2 in the air. It's perfect for soft, porous stones like sandstone and coral. Hydraulic lime sets by reaction with water and can set underwater; it's better for damp conditions or hard stones like granite. For most African restoration, NHL 3.5 is a good all-rounder.

Mix lime mortar properly. For NHL: use 1 part lime to 2.5 parts sharp sand by volume. For lime putty: 1 part putty to 3 parts sand. Add water slowly â the mix should be like thick porridge. Let it stand for 15 minutes, then remix. Never add cement, as it defeats the purpose. Use clean, well-graded sand (0-4 mm) â avoid salty beach sand unless washed.

Apply mortar in layers no thicker than 20 mm. For deep joints, build up in 10 mm layers, letting each layer firm up for a few hours. Compact well with a chisel or trowel. Finish with a wood float or stiff brush to match the original texture. Cure slowly: keep damp for 3-7 days. In hot climates, cover with damp burlap and mist twice daily.

Lime mortar is forgiving â you can rework it for hours. It also allows future removal without damaging stone. By using lime, you preserve not just the wall but the traditional craft.

lessons.title: Waterproofing and Sealing Stone Surfaces
lessons.body:
Water is the enemy of stone. It causes erosion, salt crystallisation, and biological growth. But sealing stone is tricky â you must not trap moisture inside. Breathable sealers are essential. Never use silicone or acrylic sealers on historic stone; they peel and trap water. Instead, use a breathable silane-siloxane sealer, diluted 1:10 with water. Apply with a low-pressure sprayer or brush, two coats, allowing 4 hours between coats. Test on a small area first.

Before sealing, clean the stone thoroughly and let it dry for at least 48 hours. Check for cracks â seal them with lime grout first. For walls that are constantly damp, consider a French drain or improved drainage at the base. In coastal Africa, salt spray is a problem: wash walls with fresh water every few months to remove salt.

Waterproofing also means repelling water at the surface. For horizontal surfaces like steps or copings, use a breathable sealer. For vertical walls, a water-repellent sealer is enough. Avoid plastic paints or cement renders â they crack and trap moisture. If you must paint, use limewash: mix 1 part lime putty with 3 parts water, add a handful of salt for adhesion. Apply two coats.

Another method is to install a damp-proof course (DPC) by cutting a slot at the base and inserting a breathable membrane. This is advanced work â call a professional. For most learners, regular maintenance: keep gutters clean, repair cracks, and reapply sealer every 5-7 years. In Africa's intense sun and rain, sealing extends stone life significantly.

lessons.title: Practical Exercise: Repointing a Stone Wall
lessons.body:
In this exercise, you will repoint a 1 m x 1 m section of an old stone wall. You need: a plugging chisel, mallet, mortar rake, stiff brush, pointing trowel, jointing tool, bucket, mixing board, and materials: NHL 3.5 lime, sharp sand, water. Choose a wall that is not load-bearing and has failing mortar â crumbly, recessed, or cracked.

Step 1: Prepare the joint. Use the plugging chisel and mallet to remove old mortar to a depth of 2-3 cm. Work vertically, not horizontally, to avoid dislodging stones. Use the mortar rake to clean sides. Brush out all dust with a stiff brush. Wet the joint with water â this prevents the new mortar from drying too fast.

Step 2: Mix mortar. On a mixing board, combine 1 part NHL 3.5 with 2.5 parts sharp sand. Add water gradually, mixing with a trowel until it holds its shape. Let it stand 10 minutes, then remix. It should be workable but not runny.

Step 3: Point the joints. Use the pointing trowel to press mortar into the joint, filling it completely. Work from bottom to top. For deep joints, fill in two stages, scratching the first layer to key the second. Finish with a jointing tool â a concave finish is traditional and sheds water. Do not over-smooth.

Step 4: Clean and cure. Remove excess mortar with a dry brush before it sets. Keep the wall damp for 3 days by misting and covering with burlap. In hot sun, mist twice daily. After 3 days, remove burlap and let it cure slowly.

Step 5: Inspect. After one week, check for cracks or shrinkage. Fill any with lime mortar. This exercise teaches the core skill of stone restoration. Repeat on different walls to master the technique.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Stone and Masonry Restoration for African Buildings

Stone and masonry restoration is one of the most bankable skills in Africa's built heritage economy. Across the continent, colonial-era administrative blocks, Swahili coral-stone houses, Ethiopian rock-hewn churches, Moroccan medina walls, and mission stations are ageing â and owners, heritage trusts, municipalities, and private investors are paying to bring them back into productive use. This practical reference gives you the field-ready knowledge to quote, plan, and execute restoration work profitably, from Cairo to Cape Town.

Africa's stone stock falls into four commercial categories: coral rag (Lamu, Zanzibar, Mombasa), sandstone (Cape Town, Timbuktu, Zimbabwe's Great Zimbabwe precinct), granite and basalt (Ethiopia, Kenya highlands, Nigeria's Jos Plateau), and laterite (West African savannah, Ghana, Burkina Faso). Each behaves differently under cleaning, repointing, and waterproofing. Knowing the stone determines your mortar, your labour rate, and your risk.

Commercial Reality: Why Masonry Restoration Sells in Africa

Three demand drivers make this a viable business line. First, heritage tourism: Zanzibar's Stone Town, Lamu Old Town, and Ghana's Cape Coast Castle all require periodic masonry conservation funded by tourism revenue and international grants. Second, adaptive reuse: developers converting old stone warehouses into boutique hotels, coworking hubs, and galleries need authentic masonry finishes. Third, climate resilience: coastal salt attack and Sahelian thermal cycling destroy weak cement repointing within a decade, creating recurring maintenance contracts.

Your margin comes from three levers: correct mortar specification (lime, not cement), efficient joint preparation, and disciplined waterproofing that does not trap moisture. Get these right and you can price at USD 25â60 per square metre of wall face in East and Southern Africa, with materials typically 20â30% of the contract value.

Table 1: Stone Types, Behaviour, and Mortar Match (Africa)

Stone Type Typical African Locations Porosity Recommended Mortar Key Risk
Coral rag / limestone Lamu, Zanzibar, Mombasa, Mozambique Island High Lime putty : sand 1:3, no cement Salt crystallisation; cement traps moisture
Sandstone Cape Town, Timbuktu, Great Zimbabwe Mediumâhigh Hydraulic lime NHL 3.5 : sand 1:3 Surface erosion; acid cleaning dissolves binder
Granite / basalt Ethiopia (Lalibela), Jos Plateau, Kenya highlands Low NHL 3.5 or weak cement-lime 1:1:6 Thermal cracking; hard mortar abrades edges
Laterite Ghana, Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria High Earth-lime 1:1:4 with local clay Water erosion; requires breathable finish

Sources: ICOMOS Illustrated Glossary on Stone Deterioration Patterns (2008); Historic England Repointing Brick and Stone Walls (2017); UNESCO World Heritage Centre site reports for Lamu, Stone Town, and Lalibela.

Table 2: Cleaning, Repointing, and Waterproofing Cost Benchmarks (2024, USD)

Task Unit Labour Rate Material Rate Notes
Gentle cleaning (brushes, poultice) mÂ² 6â12 2â4 No abrasive blasting on coral or sandstone
Joint raking and repointing mÂ² 18â35 4â8 Depth 15â25 mm; lime mortar only
Stone replacement (matched) mÂ² 40â90 20â60 Quarry matching is the cost driver
Breathable waterproofing (silane/siloxane) mÂ² 5â10 6â14 Vapour-permeable only; never film-forming

Sources: East African heritage contractor quotes (2024); Historic England Repointing Brick and Stone Walls (2017); RICS Africa construction cost data 2024.

â  SAFETY WARNING â SILICA DUST AND LEAD PAINT

Raking, cutting, and brushing historic masonry releases crystalline silica dust, a confirmed cause of silicosis and lung cancer. In older African buildings, paint and mortar may also contain lead (pre-1970s) or asbestos fibres. Always: (1) wear a P2/P3 respirator, sealed goggles, and gloves; (2) wet the joint before raking to suppress dust; (3) never dry-sweep or use compressed air; (4) test paint for lead before disturbing; (5) provide on-site washing facilities and change contaminated clothing before leaving site. Non-compliance can shut down your contract and expose you to legal liability.

Field Method: The Six-Step Repointing Sequence

  1. Survey and record. Photograph every elevation, map cracks, and note stone types. This becomes your variation-order evidence.
  2. Rake the joint. Remove decayed mortar to 15â25 mm depth using hand chisels or a low-speed grinder with a diamond blade. Stop at sound mortar.
  3. Clean and pre-wet. Brush out dust, then dampen the joint to prevent the new mortar drying too fast â critical in African heat.
  4. Mix lime mortar. For coral and sandstone: 1 part lime putty to 3 parts well-graded sand. For granite: NHL 3.5 at 1:3. Add water sparingly.
  5. Pack in layers. Fill in 10 mm lifts, compacting each with a chisel or pointing iron. Finish flush or slightly recessed to match historic profile.
  6. Cure slowly. Keep damp for 3â7 days using hessian or misting. Never let lime mortar dry out in direct sun.

Waterproofing That Does Not Destroy the Wall

The cardinal rule: historic stone walls must breathe. Film-forming sealers (acrylics, silicone emulsions) trap moisture and cause spalling â a costly failure you will be called back to fix. Specify vapour-permeable silane or siloxane breathable water repellents, applied to saturated but surface-dry stone at manufacturer's coverage. In coastal Africa, reapply every 5â7 years; build this into your maintenance contract as recurring revenue.

Quick Reference Checklist

  • Identify the stone type before specifying any mortar or cleaner.
  • Never use Portland cement mortar on coral, sandstone, or laterite.
  • Rake joints to 15â25 mm; stop at sound mortar.
  • Pre-wet joints and cure lime mortar damp for 3â7 days.
  • Match mortar strength, colour, and texture to the historic fabric.
  • Use only breathable, vapour-permeable waterproofing.
  • Wear P2/P3 respiratory protection; suppress dust with water.
  • Photograph every stage for client sign-off and variation claims.

Further Reading (Free Official Sources)

  • Historic England â Repointing Brick and Stone Walls: historicengland.org.uk
  • ICOMOS â Illustrated Glossary on Stone Deterioration Patterns: icomos.org
  • UNESCO World Heritage Centre â Managing Disaster Risks for World Heritage: whc.unesco.org
  • Getty Conservation Institute â Stone Conservation: An Overview of Current Research: getty.edu
  • African World Heritage Fund â Technical guidance and project reports: awhf.net

Business takeaway: Stone and masonry restoration is not a charity project â it is a repeatable, high-margin service for heritage tourism, adaptive reuse, and climate resilience. Master lime mortar, breathable waterproofing, and disciplined documentation, and you can build a restoration firm that African property owners call first.

quiz.q: What is the first step before restoring any old stone wall?
options: B) Identify stone and mortar types
quiz.explanation: Identifying materials ensures you use compatible repair methods and avoid damage.

quiz.q: Which stone is typically soft and porous?
quiz.explanation: Sandstone is sedimentary and easily scratched, while granite is hard and igneous.

quiz.q: How can you test if mortar is lime-based?
quiz.explanation: Lime mortar fizzes when vinegar (acid) is applied due to calcium carbonate.

quiz.q: Why is cement mortar harmful to historic stone?
options: B) It traps moisture and cracks stone
quiz.explanation: Cement is harder and less breathable than lime, causing spalling and moisture damage.

quiz.q: What tool should never be used to clean old stone?
quiz.explanation: High-pressure washing erodes stone and forces water into cracks.

quiz.q: When repointing, how deep should you remove old mortar?
quiz.explanation: Removing 2-3 cm provides enough depth for new mortar to key in.

quiz.q: What is the correct mix ratio for NHL lime mortar?
quiz.explanation: A 1:2.5 ratio of NHL to sharp sand is standard for repointing.

quiz.q: Why should you not smooth mortar with a metal trowel?
options: B) It seals the surface and prevents breathability
quiz.explanation: Metal troweling compresses the mortar, reducing its ability to allow moisture to escape.

quiz.q: What is the best finish for repointed joints?
quiz.explanation: A concave finish sheds water and matches traditional profiles.

quiz.q: How long should you keep new lime mortar damp?
quiz.explanation: Damping for 3 days slows curing and prevents shrinkage cracks.

quiz.q: What should you do before setting a replacement stone?
quiz.explanation: Soaking prevents the stone from absorbing moisture from the mortar.

quiz.q: How wide a crack can be left if stable?
quiz.explanation: Hairline cracks under 1 mm are usually stable and can be monitored.

quiz.q: What is the best way to remove a damaged stone?
options: B) Chisel and mallet from centre out
quiz.explanation: Working from the centre outwards avoids damaging adjacent stones.

quiz.q: What type of lime sets by carbonation?
quiz.explanation: Non-hydraulic lime (lime putty) hardens by reacting with carbon dioxide.

quiz.q: Which lime is best for damp conditions?
quiz.explanation: Hydraulic lime can set in damp conditions and is more durable.

quiz.q: What sand should be used for lime mortar?
quiz.explanation: Sharp sand provides strength and breathability; beach sand may contain salt.

quiz.q: What is a breathable sealer?
quiz.explanation: Silane-siloxane sealers repel water while allowing vapour to escape.

quiz.q: How often should breathable sealer be reapplied?
quiz.explanation: Most breathable sealers degrade after 5-7 years and need reapplication.

quiz.q: What is limewash made of?
quiz.explanation: Limewash is a traditional breathable coating of lime putty, water, and sometimes salt.

quiz.q: Why avoid plastic paint on historic stone?
quiz.explanation: Plastic paint is non-breathable and can cause blistering and stone decay.

quiz.q: What is the first step in the practical repointing exercise?
quiz.explanation: Removing old mortar to the correct depth is essential before repointing.

quiz.q: What tool is used to remove old mortar?
quiz.explanation: A plugging chisel and mallet are designed for cutting out mortar joints.

quiz.q: How should mortar be applied in deep joints?
quiz.explanation: Building up in layers ensures proper compaction and avoids shrinkage.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of scratching the first layer of mortar?
options: A) To make it look rough
B) To key the second layer
quiz.explanation: Scratching provides a mechanical key for the next layer to bond.

quiz.q: How long should you wait before inspecting the repointed wall?
quiz.explanation: After one week, the mortar has set enough to check for cracks.

quiz.q: What is a sign of good lime mortar?
options: A) It sets hard like cement
quiz.explanation: Lime mortar remains slightly flexible, accommodating movement without cracking.

quiz.q: Which stone is common along the Swahili coast?
quiz.explanation: Coral rag is a traditional building stone in East African coastal areas.

quiz.q: What is laterite?
quiz.explanation: Laterite is a reddish, iron-rich stone formed in tropical climates.

quiz.q: What is the best way to test stone hardness?
quiz.explanation: A pocket knife scratch test indicates relative hardness (Mohs scale).

quiz.q: Why is it important to match replacement stone to original?
options: B) For compatibility of hardness and porosity
quiz.explanation: Mismatched stone can cause differential movement and damage.
